claim: Head and neck cancer (HNC) is the sixth most common malignancy worldwide.
source: Head and neck cancer (HNC) is the sixth most common malignancy worldwide (Lindsey et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lindsey et al., 2012

claim: Irradiation (IR) is an important treatment approach for HNC.
source: Irradiation (IR) is an important treatment approach for HNC.

claim: Salivary glands are highly radiosensitive.
source: Salivary glands, which are often included in the IR field, are highly radiosensitive, and IR often results in salivary gland hypofunction.

claim: IR often results in salivary gland hypofunction.
source: Salivary glands, which are often included in the IR field, are highly radiosensitive, and IR often results in salivary gland hypofunction.
evidence: Based on established medical knowledge

claim: IR destroys salivary gland acinar cells, resulting in xerostomia.
source: IR destroys salivary gland acinar cells, the sole site of fluid transport in the gland parenchyma, resulting in xerostomia, which severely impacts quality of life for affected patients (Bhide et al., 2009; Davies and Thompson, 2015; Mercadante et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bhide et al., 2009; Davies and Thompson, 2015; Mercadante et al., 2017

claim: Acinar cells are the sole site of fluid transport in the gland parenchyma.
source: IR destroys salivary gland acinar cells, the sole site of fluid transport in the gland parenchyma, resulting in xerostomia, which severely impacts quality of life for affected patients (Bhide et al., 2009; Davies and Thompson, 2015; Mercadante et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on established anatomical knowledge

claim: Serous acinar cells are much more radiosensitive than mucous acinar cells.
source: Serous acinar cells are much more radiosensitive than mucous acinar cells.
evidence: Based on established biological knowledge

claim: The parotid gland consists solely of serous acinar cells.
source: Notably, the parotid gland consists solely of serous acinar cells, which makes the parotid gland more radiosensitive than the submandibular and sublingual gland (Grundmann et al., 2009).

claim: The parotid gland is more radiosensitive than the submandibular and sublingual gland.
source: Notably, the parotid gland consists solely of serous acinar cells, which makes the parotid gland more radiosensitive than the submandibular and sublingual gland (Grundmann et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Grundmann et al., 2009 and logical inference from the composition of cell types

claim: The parotid gland provides an excellent model organ to study IR-induced salivary gland hypofunction.
source: As such, the parotid gland provides an excellent model organ to study IR-induced salivary gland hypofunction.
evidence: Inferred from the high radiosensitivity of the parotid gland

claim: Most treatment modalities for xerostomia are therapeutic and beneficial for patients with established xerostomia.
source: However, most of these treatment modalities are therapeutic and thus beneficial for patients with established xerostomia (i.e., when salivary glands are severely damaged) and have not been adequately resolved IR-induced xerostomia (Vissink et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vissink et al., 2010

claim: Current treatment modalities have not adequately resolved IR-induced xerostomia.
source: However, most of these treatment modalities are therapeutic and thus beneficial for patients with established xerostomia (i.e., when salivary glands are severely damaged) and have not been adequately resolved IR-induced xerostomia (Vissink et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vissink et al., 2010

claim: There have been no studies on the prevention of IR-induced xerostomia.
source: In addition, there have been no studies on the prevention of IR-induced xerostomia.
evidence: Based on literature review by the authors

claim: At least 25% of circulating nitrate is actively taken up by salivary glands.
source: At least 25% of circulating nitrate is actively taken up by salivary glands (via sialin) and secreted into saliva, such that the concentration of nitrate in saliva is approximately tenfold greater than that in blood (Omar et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Omar et al., 2016

claim: The concentration of nitrate in saliva is approximately tenfold greater than that in blood.
source: At least 25% of circulating nitrate is actively taken up by salivary glands (via sialin) and secreted into saliva, such that the concentration of nitrate in saliva is approximately tenfold greater than that in blood (Omar et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Omar et al., 2016

claim: Nitrate has been shown to offer protection against diseases such as obesity, diabetes mellitus, and heart disease.
source: Nitrate has been shown to offer protection against diseases such as obesity, diabetes mellitus, and heart disease (Gilchrist et al., 2014; Khambata et al., 2017; Kina-Tanada et al., 2017; Lundberg et al., 2018; Ma et al., 2018; McNally et al., 2016; Omar et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Sialin (Slc17a5) is a transmembrane protein expressed most abundantly in the acinar cells of the parotid gland.
source: Sialin (Slc17a5) is a transmembrane protein expressed most abundantly in the acinar cells of the parotid gland (Qin et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Qin et al., 2012

claim: Sialin transports nitrate and other essential cellular substances such as glutamate and aspartate.
source: Sialin transports nitrate and other essential cellular substances such as glutamate and aspartate, and contributes to the maintenance of acinar cells physiological function (Qin et al., 2012).

claim: Sialin contributes to the maintenance of acinar cells physiological function.
source: Sialin transports nitrate and other essential cellular substances such as glutamate and aspartate, and contributes to the maintenance of acinar cells physiological function (Qin et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Qin et al., 2012

claim: The parotid glands of mice and rats are not similar to those of humans.
source: The parotid glands of mice and rats are not similar to those of humans (Wang et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 1998

claim: The parotid glands of miniature pigs have similar anatomical and physiological characteristics to those of human parotid glands.
source: We previously demonstrated that the parotid glands of miniature pigs have similar anatomical and physiological characteristics to those of human parotid glands.
evidence: Based on previous work by the authors

claim: A miniature pig model of IR-induced parotid gland hypofunction was established using single-dose or fractionated IR.
source: Then we established miniature pig model of IR-induced parotid gland hypofunction using single-dose or fractionated IR (Guo et al., 2014; Li et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Guo et al., 2014; Li et al., 2005

claim: Preventive nitrate administration maintained salivary flow rate in miniature pigs after IR.
source: In the preventive nitrate group, the mean SFR was significantly decreased at 1-month post-IR, but recovered to nearly normal levels at 4 months post-IR. Long-term observation (2 years post-IR) showed that SFR was at 80% of pre-IR levels (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b

claim: Therapeutic nitrate administration did not significantly recover salivary flow rate in miniature pigs after IR.
source: However, the mean SFR in the therapeutic nitrate group did not show significant recovery and remained similar to that in the IR control group (Figure 1e).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e

claim: Preventive nitrate administration maintained local blood flow rate in irradiated parotid glands.
source: Local blood flow rate was stable in the preventive nitrate group post-IR, but decreased sharply with time in the therapeutic and IR control groups (Figure 1c and f).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1c and 1f

claim: Far more acinar cells remained and less fibrosis was present at 4 months post-IR in the preventive nitrate group compared to the therapeutic and control groups.
source: Histological analyses showed that far more acinar cells remained and less fibrosis was present at 4 months post-IR in the preventive nitrate group compared to the therapeutic and control groups (Figure 1g).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 1g

claim: Exogenously administered nitrate was well absorbed, as evidenced by significantly higher salivary and serum nitrate concentrations in the nitrate groups.
source: Exogenously administered nitrate was well absorbed, as evidenced by significantly higher salivary and serum nitrate concentrations in the nitrate groups compared with those in the control groups. This difference was more pronounced at higher nitrate doses (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, b

claim: Nitrate protected salivary flow rate from IR-induced changes in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Conversely, mean SFRs were protected from IR-induced changes in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b

claim: The highest mean SFR was observed in the group that received 2 mmol/kg∙day nitrate, with a mean SFR of nearly 85% of the pre-IR SFR.
source: The highest mean SFR was observed in the group that received 2 mmol/kg∙day nitrate, with a mean SFR of nearly 85% of the pre-IR SFR.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Nitrate reduced irradiated parotid gland weight in a dose-dependent manner.
source: In addition, nitrate reduced irradiated parotid gland weight in a dose-dependent manner, and there was no significant difference between parotid gland weights in the highest-dose group (2 mmol/kg∙day) and the sham group (Figure 2d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d

claim: Parotid gland morphology was generally maintained in the nitrate groups in a dose-dependent manner.
source: However, parotid gland morphology was generally maintained in the nitrate groups in a dose-dependent manner. In the highest-dose group (2 mmol/kg∙day), the morphology was nearly identical to that of the sham group (Figure 2e).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 2e

claim: Nitrate contributed to the preservation of function and morphology in irradiated parotid glands in a dose-dependent manner.
source: These results demonstrated that nitrate contributed to the preservation of function and morphology in irradiated parotid glands in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results on SFR, weight, and morphology

claim: Nitrate administration significantly increased the proliferation of acinar and ductal cells as determined by Ki67 expression.
source: Nitrate administration significantly increased the proliferation of acinar and ductal cells as determined by Ki67 expression (Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 3a

claim: Microvessel density was significantly increased following nitrate administration.
source: Furthermore, microvessel density (MVD; measured by CD31 expression) was significantly increased following nitrate administration, whereas the IR control group showed marked MVD loss (Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 3b

claim: Aquaporin 5 (AQP5) was highly expressed in the acini of the nitrate group.
source: Aquaporin 5 (AQP5), a water channel essential for saliva secretion, was highly expressed in the acini of the nitrate group (Figure 3c), further suggesting that the secretory function of the remaining parotid gland tissue was preserved in response to nitrate administration.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 3c

claim: Sialin expression was increased after nitrate administration.
source: Surprisingly, sialin expression was increased after nitrate administration (Figure 3d), suggesting there is a close interaction between sialin and nitrate.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical and western blot data shown in Figure 3d

claim: Nitrate had a dose-dependent positive effect on sialin expression in human parotid gland cells in vitro.
source: Moreover, the results of nitrate administration to human parotid gland cells (hPGCs) in vitro confirmed that nitrate had a dose-dependent positive effect on sialin expression (Figure 3e and f, Figure 3—source data 1 and Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR and western blot data shown in Figures 3e and 3f

claim: Nitrate administration prior to IR significantly increased cell proliferation in hPGCs.
source: We found that nitrate administration prior to IR (Figure 4a) significantly increased cell proliferation (Figure 4b and c), but little effect on cell apoptosis (Figure 4d).
evidence: Supported by CCK-8 and EdU staining data shown in Figures 4b and 4c

claim: Nitrate administration to hPGCs resulted in a dose-dependent increase in sialin expression.
source: Moreover, nitrate administration to hPGCs in vitro resulted in a dose-dependent increase in sialin expression (Figure 4e and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR and western blot data shown in Figure 4e

claim: Slc17a5 knockdown led to significantly reduced cell proliferation.
source: We found that Slc17a5 knockdown led to significantly reduced cell proliferation, and Slc17a5 overexpression resulted in a small, but significant, increase in proliferation (Figure 4g and h).
evidence: Supported by CCK-8 and EdU staining data shown in Figures 4g and 4h

claim: Slc17a5 overexpression resulted in a small, but significant, increase in proliferation.
source: We found that Slc17a5 knockdown led to significantly reduced cell proliferation, and Slc17a5 overexpression resulted in a small, but significant, increase in proliferation (Figure 4g and h).
evidence: Supported by CCK-8 and EdU staining data shown in Figures 4g and 4h

claim: Sialin-mediated nitrate transportation promoted hPGCs proliferation.
source: These findings indicated that sialin-mediated nitrate transportation promoted hPGCs proliferation.
evidence: Inferred from the knockdown and overexpression experiments

claim: Slc17a5 knockdown prolonged the G1 phase, and shortened the S and G2/M phases.
source: Cell cycle analysis indicated that Slc17a5 knockdown prolonged the G1 phase, and shortened the S and G2/M phases (Figure 4i), resulting in G1 to S phase arrest.
evidence: Supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 4i

claim: Slc17a5 knockdown resulted in increased apoptosis.
source: Furthermore, Slc17a5 knockdown resulted in increased apoptosis (Figure 4j).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4j

claim: Cells derived from the submandibular glands of Slc17a5 knockdown mice exhibited a significantly lower proliferation rate than cells derived from wild-type mice.
source: Cells derived from the submandibular glands of Slc17a5 knockdown mice (sgRNA two-cell embryo) showed decreased nitrate secretion and exhibited a significantly lower proliferation rate that that of cells derived from wild-type (WT) mice (Figure 4k and l); this further supports the conclusion that sialin-mediated nitrate transportation promoted cell proliferation.
evidence: Supported by CCK-8 and EdU staining data shown in Figures 4k and 4l

claim: SialinH183R could not increase cell proliferation similar to WT sialin.
source: We overexpressed sialinH183R (Figure 4m) and found that sialinH183R could not increase cell proliferation similar to WT sialin (Figure 4n).
evidence: Supported by CCK-8 data shown in Figure 4n

claim: Nitrate could increase sialin expression in parotid gland cells, creating a nitrate-sialin feedback loop.
source: These results demonstrated that nitrate could increase sialin expression in parotid gland cells, creating a nitrate-sialin feedback loop, and that sialin-mediated nitrate transportation is essential to maintain cell survival, promote parotid gland cell proliferation, and inhibit apoptosis.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results showing nitrate increases sialin expression and sialin facilitates nitrate transport

claim: Sialin-mediated nitrate transportation is essential to maintain cell survival, promote parotid gland cell proliferation, and inhibit apoptosis.
source: These results demonstrated that nitrate could increase sialin expression in parotid gland cells, creating a nitrate-sialin feedback loop, and that sialin-mediated nitrate transportation is essential to maintain cell survival, promote parotid gland cell proliferation, and inhibit apoptosis.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results on cell proliferation and apoptosis

claim: Nitrate plays a dominant role in preventing IR damage and sialin acts as a nitrate transporter.
source: Sialin acts as a transporter in IR protection in which nitrate plays a dominant role. It is the sialin-meditated nitrate transportation that protects salivary glands from IR damage.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results showing sialinH183R mutation cannot increase proliferation

claim: IR of hPGCs significantly impaired proliferation.
source: IR of hPGCs significantly impaired proliferation (Figure 5a–c), and increased apoptosis (Figure 5d).
evidence: Supported by CCK-8 and EdU staining data shown in Figures 5b and 5c

claim: IR of hPGCs increased apoptosis.
source: IR of hPGCs significantly impaired proliferation (Figure 5a–c), and increased apoptosis (Figure 5d).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5d

claim: Sialin expression progressively and significantly decreased in hPGCs over time following IR.
source: Sialin expression progressively and significantly decreased in hPGCs over time following IR, which showed that sialin is markedly affected by IR (Figure 5e and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR and western blot data shown in Figure 5e

claim: Slc17a5 knockdown with siRNA and subsequent 5 Gy IR significantly impaired cell proliferation.
source: Slc17a5 knockdown with siRNA and subsequent 5 Gy IR (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a, b, Figure 5—figure supplement 1—source data 1) significantly impaired cell proliferation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c,d) and increased apoptosis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: Supported by EdU staining and CCK-8 data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1c,d

claim: Slc17a5 knockdown with siRNA and subsequent 5 Gy IR increased apoptosis.
source: Slc17a5 knockdown with siRNA and subsequent 5 Gy IR (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a, b, Figure 5—figure supplement 1—source data 1) significantly impaired cell proliferation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c,d) and increased apoptosis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1e

claim: Slc17a5 overexpression preserved cell proliferation after IR.
source: Conversely, Slc17a5 overexpression (Figure 5e, f, g, Figure 5—source data 2) that facilitated nitrate transportation preserved cell proliferation (Figure 5h and i) and counteracted IR-induced cell apoptosis (Figure 5j).
evidence: Supported by CCK-8 and EdU staining data shown in Figures 5h and 5i

claim: Slc17a5 overexpression counteracted IR-induced cell apoptosis.
source: Conversely, Slc17a5 overexpression (Figure 5e, f, g, Figure 5—source data 2) that facilitated nitrate transportation preserved cell proliferation (Figure 5h and i) and counteracted IR-induced cell apoptosis (Figure 5j).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5j

claim: Reduced sialin expression worsened IR damage.
source: These results suggested that reduced sialin expression worsened IR damage, and that maintenance of sialin expression for nitrate transportation could promote cell proliferation and inhibit IR-induced apoptosis.
evidence: Inferred from the knockdown experiments showing increased damage with reduced sialin

claim: Maintenance of sialin expression for nitrate transportation could promote cell proliferation and inhibit IR-induced apoptosis.
source: These results suggested that reduced sialin expression worsened IR damage, and that maintenance of sialin expression for nitrate transportation could promote cell proliferation and inhibit IR-induced apoptosis.
evidence: Inferred from the overexpression experiments showing protection with increased sialin

claim: Nitrate administration upregulated EGFR.
source: After nitrate administration, EGFR was significantly upregulated, which indicated that the EGFR signaling pathway was activated (Figure 6a and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6a

claim: Nitrate administration activated the EGFR signaling pathway.
source: After nitrate administration, EGFR was significantly upregulated, which indicated that the EGFR signaling pathway was activated (Figure 6a and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Inferred from the upregulation of EGFR

claim: Nitrate administration increased phosphorylation of EGFR, AKT, and ERK.
source: We found that nitrate administration increased phosphorylation of EGFR, AKT, and ERK (Figure 6a and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6a

claim: Blockade of EGFR attenuated nitrate-mediated promotion of cell proliferation.
source: Blockade of EGFR attenuated nitrate-mediated promotion of cell proliferation (Figure 6b).
evidence: Supported by CCK-8 data shown in Figure 6b

claim: Blockade of EGFR inhibited phosphorylation of AKT and ERK.
source: Moreover, blockade of EGFR inhibited phosphorylation of AKT and ERK; nitrate administration reversed this effect (Figure 6c and Figure 6—source data 2), which indicated that EGFR was upstream of both the AKT and MAPK signaling pathways.
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6c

claim: Nitrate administration reversed the inhibition of AKT and ERK phosphorylation caused by EGFR blockade.
source: Moreover, blockade of EGFR inhibited phosphorylation of AKT and ERK; nitrate administration reversed this effect (Figure 6c and Figure 6—source data 2), which indicated that EGFR was upstream of both the AKT and MAPK signaling pathways.
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6c

claim: EGFR is upstream of both the AKT and MAPK signaling pathways.
source: Moreover, blockade of EGFR inhibited phosphorylation of AKT and ERK; nitrate administration reversed this effect (Figure 6c and Figure 6—source data 2), which indicated that EGFR was upstream of both the AKT and MAPK signaling pathways.
evidence: Inferred from the EGFR blockade experiments

claim: Knockdown of sialin prevented nitrate-induced activation of EGFR.
source: Notably, knockdown of sialin prevented nitrate-induced activation of EGFR suggesting that nitrate-mediated regulation of the EGFR signaling pathway required sialin (Figure 6a and Figure 6—source data 3).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6a

claim: Nitrate-mediated regulation of the EGFR signaling pathway required sialin.
source: Notably, knockdown of sialin prevented nitrate-induced activation of EGFR suggesting that nitrate-mediated regulation of the EGFR signaling pathway required sialin (Figure 6a and Figure 6—source data 3).
evidence: Inferred from the sialin knockdown experiments

claim: Sialin expression was decreased after NO was blocked by PTIO.
source: Sialin expression was decreased after NO was blocked by PTIO (Figure 6d and Figure 6—source data 4).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6d

claim: EGFR phosphorylation was decreased after NO scavenging.
source: We also found that EGFR phosphorylation was decreased after NO scavenging (Figure 6d and Figure 6—source data 4).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6d

claim: Nitrate increases sialin expression and EGFR phosphorylation via the NO pathway.
source: We have demonstrated that nitrate increases sialin expression and EGFR phosphorylation via the NO pathway and thus regulates EGFR-AKT-MAPK signaling pathway.
evidence: Inferred from the PTIO experiments showing decreased sialin and EGFR phosphorylation when NO is blocked

claim: Significantly elevated phosphorylation of EGFR, AKT, and ERK was observed in the nitrate group in vivo compared with the IR control and sham groups.
source: Moreover, we have also observed significantly elevated phosphorylation of EGFR, AKT, and ERK in the nitrate group in vivo compared with the IR control and sham groups that were consistent with our in vitro study (Figure 6e and Figure 6—source data 5).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6e

claim: A nitrate-sialin feedback loop could mediate cell proliferation to protect the parotid gland from IR damage via the EGFR–AKT–MAPK signaling pathway.
source: These results suggested that a nitrate-sialin feedback loop could mediate cell proliferation to protect the parotid gland from IR damage via the EGFR–AKT–MAPK signaling pathway (Figure 6f).
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of all experiments

claim: Dietary nitrate administration protected the parotid gland against IR damage in a dose-dependent manner.
source: In this study, we demonstrated that dietary nitrate administration protected the parotid gland against IR damage in a dose-dependent manner, by using an established miniature pig model of IR-induced parotid gland hypofunction.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the miniature pig model

claim: Nitrate supplementation enhanced hPGCs cell proliferation via EGFR–AKT–MAPK signaling pathway.
source: We found that nitrate supplementation enhanced hPGCs cell proliferation via EGFR–AKT–MAPK signaling pathway.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from in vitro studies

claim: Dietary nitrate administration may be an effective novel approach for the prevention of IR-induced xerostomia.
source: Therefore, dietary nitrate administration may be an effective novel approach for the prevention of IR-induced xerostomia.
evidence: Speculative conclusion based on the experimental results

claim: Nitrate increased serous acinar and ductal cell proliferation rates.
source: In the present study, nitrate increased serous acinar and ductal cell proliferation rates, and increased MVD.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Nitrate increased microvessel density (MVD).
source: In the present study, nitrate increased serous acinar and ductal cell proliferation rates, and increased MVD.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Increased cell proliferation, MVD, and other parameters are crucial for maintenance of salivary gland homeostasis and restoration of function.
source: Each of these parameters is crucial for maintenance of salivary gland homeostasis and restoration of function (Aure et al., 2015; Ekström et al., 2017; Weng et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aure et al., 2015; Ekström et al., 2017; Weng et al., 2018

claim: There is a close interaction between nitrate and sialin in vivo and in vitro, demonstrating a nitrate-sialin feedback loop.
source: We showed a close interaction between nitrate and sialin in vivo using a miniature pig model and in vitro using hPGCs, demonstrating a nitrate-sialin feedback loop in which the nitrate increased sialin expression and sialin facilitated nitrate influx into cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from both in vivo and in vitro studies

claim: Preventive nitrate administration increased sialin expression, promoted acinar and ductal cell proliferation, and reduced apoptosis via the EGFR–AKT–MAPK signaling pathway.
source: Preventive nitrate administration increased sialin expression, promoted acinar and ductal cell proliferation, and reduced apoptosis via the EGFR–AKT–MAPK signaling pathway.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Nitrate administration could not reverse IR-induced damage when sialin expression was sharply reduced.
source: However, nitrate administration could not reverse IR-induced damage when sialin expression was sharply reduced.

claim: Preventive, but not therapeutic, nitrate administration was effective in the in vivo large animal study.
source: These findings explained why preventive, but not therapeutic, nitrate administration was effective in our in vivo large animal study.

claim: Clinical trials showed positive effects of hAQP1 gene transfer therapy.
source: Clinical trials showed positive effects of hAQP1 gene transfer therapy (Alevizos et al., 2017; Baum et al., 2012; Baum et al., 2010), which exhibited beneficial effects in patients with established xerostomia (i.e., when the salivary glands already were severely damaged), but did not totally resolve IR induced xerostomia.
evidence: Supported by citations to Alevizos et al., 2017; Baum et al., 2012; Baum et al., 2010

claim: hAQP1 gene transfer therapy did not totally resolve IR induced xerostomia.
source: Clinical trials showed positive effects of hAQP1 gene transfer therapy (Alevizos et al., 2017; Baum et al., 2012; Baum et al., 2010), which exhibited beneficial effects in patients with established xerostomia (i.e., when the salivary glands already were severely damaged), but did not totally resolve IR induced xerostomia.
evidence: Supported by citations to Alevizos et al., 2017; Baum et al., 2012; Baum et al., 2010

claim: Nitrate administration resulted in preservation of approximately 85% of secretory function at the highest dose (2 mmol/kg∙day) in miniature pigs.
source: In miniature pigs, nitrate administration resulted in preservation of approximately 85% of secretory function and maintenance of nearly normal morphology at the highest dose provided in this study (2 mmol/kg∙day).
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Nitrate administration resulted in maintenance of nearly normal morphology at the highest dose (2 mmol/kg∙day) in miniature pigs.
source: In miniature pigs, nitrate administration resulted in preservation of approximately 85% of secretory function and maintenance of nearly normal morphology at the highest dose provided in this study (2 mmol/kg∙day).
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Nitrate administration contributed to maintenance of levels of saliva constituents (e.g., amylase).
source: In addition, nitrate administration contributed to maintenance of levels of saliva constituents (e.g., amylase).
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Inorganic nitrate lacks immunogenicity, is not subject to tolerance, is not toxic, and does not induce significant side effects at the doses employed.
source: Furthermore, inorganic nitrate lacks immunogenicity, is not subject to tolerance, is not toxic, and does not induce significant side effects at the doses employed (Omar et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Omar et al., 2012

claim: Recent studies failed to provide evidence that nitrate is a potential carcinogen.
source: However, recent studies failed to provide evidence for this assumption (Bryan et al., 2012; Hezel et al., 2015; Khambata et al., 2017; McNally et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2013; Xie et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: The World Health Organization stated that nitrate is not carcinogenic, based on both laboratory animal studies and epidemiological studies.
source: In 2011, the World Health Organization published a guideline regarding nitrate and nitrite in drinking water which stated that nitrate is not carcinogenic, based on both laboratory animal studies and epidemiological studies (World Health Organization, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2011

claim: Organic nitrate has several notable disadvantages that limit its application in the clinic.
source: Although organic nitrate has been used for the treatment of cardiovascular disease (Omar et al., 2016), it has several notable disadvantages that limit its application in the clinic (Omar et al., 2012), which include poor absorption, low oral bioavailability due to first-pass metabolism in the liver, better effectiveness via sublingual, transdermal, or rectal administration, short half-life, development of tolerance resulting from long-term administration, and side effects such as headache and postural hypotension.
evidence: Supported by citation to Omar et al., 2012

claim: Inorganic nitrate has a simple ionic structure that is easily absorbed, exhibits high oral bioavailability, has a long half-life, and causes no side effects.
source: Conversely, inorganic nitrate has a simple ionic structure that is easily absorbed, exhibits high oral bioavailability, has a long half-life, and causes no side effects (Khambata et al., 2017; Qin et al., 2012; Xia et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Khambata et al., 2017; Qin et al., 2012; Xia et al., 2015

claim: Inorganic nitrate appears to comprise a safe and effective treatment for IR-induced salivary gland hypofunction.
source: Therefore, inorganic nitrate appears to comprise a safe and effective treatment for IR-induced salivary gland hypofunction.
evidence: Speculative conclusion based on the experimental results and properties of inorganic nitrate

claim: Dietary nitrate can be metabolized into nitric oxide (NO) via the nitrate–nitrite–NO pathway.
source: Dietary nitrate can be metabolized into nitric oxide (NO) via the nitrate–nitrite–NO pathway (Lundberg et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lundberg et al., 2008

claim: NO is an important gaseous signaling molecule that participates in many physiological processes, including stimulation of reparative angiogenesis and reduction of oxidative stress.
source: NO is an important gaseous signaling molecule that participates in many physiological processes, including stimulation of reparative angiogenesis and reduction of oxidative stress (Sengupta et al., 2004; Sessa, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sengupta et al., 2004; Sessa, 2009

claim: Under hypoxic or acidic conditions, NO synthesis primarily occurs via the nitrate–nitrite–NO exogenous pathway.
source: Under hypoxic or acidic conditions, NO synthesis primarily occurs via the nitrate–nitrite–NO exogenous pathway.
evidence: Based on established biochemical knowledge

claim: IR induces a hypoxic and acidic environment within salivary glands.
source: Notably, IR induces a hypoxic and acidic environment within salivary glands.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about radiation effects

claim: Dietary nitrate supplementation results in NO production and reduces hypoxia by inducing a prolonged increase in blood flow.
source: Dietary nitrate supplementation results in NO production and reduces hypoxia by inducing a prolonged increase in blood flow (Lundberg et al., 2008), and increased gland microvascularization, which is beneficial for production of saliva by acinar cells.

claim: Nitrate-mediated NO formation increases sialin expression and upregulates EGFR-AKT-MAPK signaling pathways.
source: Furthermore, nitrate-mediated NO formation also increases sialin expression and upregulates EGFR-AKT-MAPK signaling pathways, the classical pathways that are responsible for promoting cell proliferation, maintaining cell survival, and preventing cell apoptosis (Sabbah et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2011).
